sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Silicone oil (SO) is a commonly used intraocular tamponade agent following complex vitreoretinal surgery (e.g., retinal detachment with proliferative vitreoretinopathy, giant retinal tears, trauma). While effective in achieving a 'flat retina,' its presence can lead to a variety of complications, notably secondary glaucoma. Silicone Oil-Induced Glaucoma (SOIG) refers to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) occurring in an eye filled with silicone oil. The scenario of a 'deep anterior chamber (AC)' typically suggests an open-angle mechanism or anterior migration of oil without significant pupillary block causing iris bombe, but careful evaluation is paramount.

content.description: Incidence of SOIG varies widely (10-56%) depending on baseline pathology (highest in trauma, PVR). Aphakic eyes have a 2-fold higher risk. Risk increases with oil duration, emulsification, inflammation, and high viscosity oil.

branches.label: Silicone Oil Migration/Emulsification
sub_branches: Direct obstruction of trabecular meshwork (TM) by oil droplets (macrophages ingest oil, block TM)
Oil in AC, blocking angle (pseudo-open angle)

branches.label: Pupillary Block Glaucoma
sub_branches: Oil trapped posterior to iris, preventing aqueous flow to AC (iris bombe, shallow AC - *less likely with deep AC*).
Oil trapped *in* AC, blocking pupil (can still have deep AC, but pupil block is primary mechanism)

branches.label: Inflammation
sub_branches: Chronic uveitis from SO (foreign body reaction), leading to TM scarring/dysfunction

branches.label: Neovascular Glaucoma
sub_branches: Underlying retinal ischemia (PDR, CRVO) exacerbated by vitrectomy or oil, leading to neovascularization of iris/angle

branches.label: Steroid-Induced Glaucoma
sub_branches: Post-operative topical or systemic corticosteroids (common after vitrectomy)

branches.label: Ghost Cell Glaucoma
sub_branches: Degenerated red blood cells (ghost cells) blocking TM (uncommon with pure SO tamponade)

rows: TM obstruction by emulsified oil/macrophages, inflammation
Oil trapping behind iris (iris bombe) or oil in AC blocking pupil
Reduced aqueous outflow from steroid use

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Often asymptomatic in early stages (slowly progressive IOP rise).
Gradual decrease in vision (due to optic neuropathy).
Ocular pain, headache (especially with acute rise).
Redness, photophobia (if significant inflammation).
Halos around lights (corneal edema).

sections.title: 6. Ocular Examination Findings
content: **IOP**: Elevated (often >25 mmHg, sometimes >40 mmHg).
**Visual Acuity**: May be reduced due to glaucoma, cataract, or underlying retinal pathology.
**Cornea**: Microcystic edema (high IOP), oil droplets on endothelium ('oil snowstorm' or 'oil bubbles'), band keratopathy (chronic cases).
**Anterior Chamber**: Deep (as per user input) or normal. May contain visible silicone oil droplets/emulsified oil, especially inferiorly. Cells/flare if inflammation.
**Iris**: Transillumination defects (if prior iridectomy), oil droplets on iris surface. Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) if chronic inflammation/angle closure.
**Lens**: Cataract (oil-induced, 'oil-bubble' cataract on posterior capsule), phacodonesis. Aphakia or pseudophakia are common post-vitrectomy.

**Gonioscopy**: Crucial. Open angle with oil droplets/emulsified oil visible in trabecular meshwork (TM) or covering the angle. PAS may be present. If pupillary block, angle may be closed (iris bombe) or open with oil in AC.
**Fundus**: Silicone oil bubble filling vitreous cavity. Optic disc cupping (C/D ratio increase), neuroretinal rim thinning, pallor. Flat retina (indicating successful primary surgery).

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Comprehensive Ocular Examination**: VA, IOP (tonometry), slit-lamp, gonioscopy, dilated fundus exam.
**2. Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT)**: To visualize angle configuration, presence of oil in angle, pupillary block, iris bombe, PAS.
**3. Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM)**: Excellent for visualizing oil in the AC, angle, ciliary body, and behind the iris, especially if media opacity prevents direct visualization.
**4. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)**: Optic disc and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) analysis to detect and monitor glaucomatous damage.
**5. Visual Field Testing (Perimetry)**: Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) 24-2 or 30-2 to assess functional glaucomatous damage. May be challenging with oil-filled eye.
**6. B-Scan Ultrasonography**: If media is opaque, to assess retinal status, presence of choroidal detachments, or oil localization.
**7. Fundus Photography**: Document optic disc appearance.

sections.title: 8. Differential Diagnosis of High IOP in SO-Filled Eye

rows: Oil in TM, emulsification, inflammation, pupillary block
Iris/angle neovascularization, underlying retinal ischemia (e.g., PDR), FFA shows NVE/NVI
Significant cells/flare, keratic precipitates, synechiae, no oil in TM
History of vitreous hemorrhage, degenerated RBCs in AC/TM
Shallow AC, anterior rotation of ciliary body, positive UBM findings
Shallow (often post-op for cataract or glaucoma surgery, rare with SO)
Shallow AC, hypotony, ciliochoroidal effusion on B-scan
Shallow (often causes hypotony, not high IOP, unless causing angle closure)

content.description: While no specific staging for SOIG, glaucoma severity is assessed by optic nerve damage (C/D ratio, RNFL thickness) and visual field loss (e.g., Hodapp-Parrish-Anderson criteria for HVF).

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Protocol
content: **Step 1: Medical Management (Initial)**

- **Topical Anti-glaucoma Meds**: Beta-blockers (Timolol 0.5% BID), alpha-agonists (Brimonidine 0.15% BID/TID), topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (Dorzolamide 2% TID, Brinzolamide 1% BID/TID). Prostaglandin analogues (Latanoprost 0.005% QD) can be used but with caution in inflammatory cases.
- **Oral Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors**: Acetazolamide (Diamox) 250 mg QID or 500 mg SR BID for acute, severe IOP spikes. Monitor electrolytes, renal function.
- **Topical Steroids**: Prednisolone acetate 1% QID or Dexamethasone 0.1% QID if significant inflammation is present. Taper as inflammation resolves.
**Step 2: Laser Treatment (If Pupillary Block)**
- **Nd:YAG Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI)**: If pupillary block is confirmed or suspected, especially if oil is behind the iris.
**Step 3: Surgical Management (If Medical/Laser Fails)**
- **Silicone Oil Removal (SOR)**: First-line surgical treatment if retina is stable. This is often curative for SOIG. Requires repeat pars plana vitrectomy.

- **Glaucoma Drainage Device (GDD) Implantation**: If SOR is not feasible (e.g., high risk of redetachment) or if SOIG persists after SOR. Ahmed Glaucoma Valve, Baerveldt Glaucoma Implant. (Often placed inferonasally to avoid superior rectus muscle which is often used for traction in VR surgery).
- **Cyclophotocoagulation (CPC)**: Transscleral (TSCPC) or Endoscopic (ECP). Reserved for refractory cases, eyes with poor visual potential, or as a temporizing measure.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques for SOIG
content: **Silicone Oil Removal (SOR)**: 23/25/27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy. Oil is aspirated using a vitrector or oil extraction cannula. Fluid-air exchange and potentially fluid-fluid exchange with balanced salt solution (BSS) follows. Endolaser may be repeated for any peripheral breaks. **Crucial**: Ensure retinal stability before SOR.
**Nd:YAG LPI**: Performed with Nd:YAG laser (energy 3-8 mJ, 1-3 shots). Aim for a patent iridotomy superiorly, away from visual axis. Consider multiple LPIs if one closes or if oil is dense.

**Glaucoma Drainage Devices (GDDs)**: Implantation of a valved (Ahmed) or non-valved (Baerveldt) shunt. Plate usually placed in superior temporal or inferior nasal quadrant. Tube inserted into AC, typically anterior to iris, away from endothelium. Careful dissection to create a scleral tunnel for the tube is essential.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Persistent High IOP**: Despite treatment, some eyes remain refractory.
**Glaucomatous Optic Neuropathy**: Irreversible vision loss.
**Corneal Decompensation**: Chronic high IOP, oil emulsification, and inflammation can lead to bullous keratopathy.
**Recurrent Retinal Detachment**: Primary risk after SOR, especially in complex cases.
**Hypotony**: A potential complication of GDDs or excessive CPC.
**Cataract Progression**: Common with SO tamponade, often requiring subsequent cataract surgery.
Prognosis is guarded, dependent on underlying pathology, duration of oil, and control of IOP. Early diagnosis and aggressive management are key.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: Acute, severe eye pain with headache and nausea.
Sudden, significant decrease in vision.
Corneal edema (hazy cornea).
IOP > 40 mmHg despite maximal topical therapy.
Iris bombe with shallow AC (indicates acute pupillary block - though less likely with 'deep AC').
Signs of acute inflammation (fibrin, hypopyon).

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Deep AC with high IOP in SO-filled eye**: Strongly suggests open-angle mechanism with TM obstruction by oil droplets or inflammation, or pupillary block with anterior migration of oil.
**Gonioscopy is MANDATORY**: To differentiate open-angle from angle-closure mechanisms and visualize oil in the angle.
**Silicone oil emulsification**: Increases with time, high viscosity oils, and inflammatory eyes. Small droplets are more occlusive to TM.
**Early SOR**: If retina is stable, SOR is the most effective treatment for SOIG.
**GDDs in SOIG**: Often required for refractory cases. Consider inferonasal placement to avoid areas compromised by prior VR surgery.
**Aggressive IOP control**: Essential to preserve optic nerve function. Don't delay surgical intervention if medical therapy fails.

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent research focuses on novel tamponade agents with lower complication rates, improved silicone oil formulations (e.g., heavier oils for inferior detachments, though these can also cause SOIG), and sustained-release IOP-lowering drugs. Studies continue to refine surgical techniques for GDDs in complex eyes, emphasizing personalized approaches based on the underlying pathology and patient comorbidities. The Silicone Oil Study (SOS) provided important insights into visual outcomes and complications of silicone oil versus gas tamponade in PVR.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Pediatric Eyes**: Higher incidence of SOIG (up to 60-70%) due to smaller eye size, higher inflammatory response, and often aphakia.
**Aphakia**: Significantly increases risk of SOIG due to easier anterior migration of oil.
**Pre-existing Glaucoma**: Patients with pre-existing glaucoma are at higher risk of worsening IOP control post-SO tamponade.
**Traumatic Eyes**: Higher risk of severe inflammation, neovascularization, and SOIG due to initial trauma.
